title: Changing a Flat Tire Safely - Including When the Jack Is Missing
summary: Step-by-step flat tire change using the jack and spare that came with your car, plus safe fallbacks (sealant kits, inflators, digging out) when the jack is missing or broken.

steps.title: Get off the road before you stop
steps.body: A flat shows up as pulling to one side, a shaking steering wheel, or a flapping sound. Turn on your hazard lights, ease off the gas, and brake gently - do not slam the brakes. Roll on to a parking lot, side street, or exit ramp if you can reach one at low speed; a few hundred yards on a flat may ruin the wheel, but a rim is cheaper than being struck on a narrow shoulder. If you must use the shoulder, pick firm, level, well-lit ground as far from the travel lanes as possible. Never try to change a tire on the traffic side of the car on a busy highway - call for help instead.

steps.title: Lock the car in place
steps.body: Put the car in Park (or in reverse gear for a manual), turn off the engine, take the keys, set the parking brake, and leave the hazards on. Have passengers get out on the side away from traffic and wait well off the road, behind a guardrail if there is one. Put on a reflective vest if you have one. Set a warning triangle, cone, or flare about 100 feet (30 m) behind the car. Block the tire diagonally opposite the flat with a wheel wedge, a brick, or a solid rock - in front of it if you are lifting the rear, behind it if you are lifting the front.

steps.title: Find the tools and read the manual
steps.body: Open the owner's manual to the tire-change page - it shows where the spare, jack, and lug wrench are stored and, most importantly, the exact jack points on the frame. Many newer cars have no spare at all; they carry a sealant bottle and a small air compressor instead (see step 7). Lay the spare flat on the ground near the work area so it cannot roll into the road. If you have a wheel lock, find the lock key, usually in the glove box or with the jack.

steps.title: Loosen the lug nuts while the tire is still on the ground
steps.body: Pop off any hubcap. With the car still resting on the flat, put the wrench on each lug nut and turn it counterclockwise a quarter to a half turn - just enough to break it free. The ground keeps the wheel from spinning. If a nut is very tight, put the wrench handle level and push down with your foot, keeping your body balanced. Do not remove the nuts yet. Loosening them after the car is up can rock it off the jack.

steps.title: Jack the car at the marked point only
steps.body: Place the jack under the metal jack point the manual shows, closest to the flat. Plastic trim, the oil pan, and suspension parts will crack or let the jack slip. Raise the car until the flat is about 6 inches (15 cm) off the ground - a spare that is fully inflated needs more clearance than the flat did. Keep every part of your body out from under the car the whole time. If the car shifts or the jack tilts, lower it right away and reposition on firmer ground. On soft dirt, put a flat board under the jack base.

steps.title: Swap the wheel and tighten in a star pattern
steps.body: Remove the lug nuts by hand and keep them in a pocket or hubcap so none roll away. Pull the flat straight toward you with a smooth motion and lay it flat - jerking it can knock the car off the jack. Lift the spare onto the studs with the valve stem facing out. Thread every nut by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then snug them in a star (crisscross) pattern. Lower the car until the tire just touches the ground, tighten firmly in the same star pattern, then lower it fully and remove the jack. Recheck the nuts after the first few miles.

steps.title: No jack or no spare: use the safest fallback
steps.body: If the jack is missing, broken, or the ground is too soft, call roadside assistance or ask another driver to lend a jack - this is the safe answer. For a small tread puncture, a sealant kit or the car's tire repair kit plus a 12-volt inflator can seal and refill the tire enough to reach a shop; follow the kit's speed limit. Sealant will not fix a sidewall cut or a blowout. As a last resort on soft dirt or sand, you can dig a pit under the flat so the wheel hangs free while the car stays on its other three wheels - dig deep enough for the taller, inflated spare, chock the other wheels, set the parking brake, and never put any part of you under the car.

steps.title: Check the spare and drive to a shop
steps.body: Check the spare's pressure with a gauge. Compact "donut" spares usually need about 60 psi - the correct number is printed on the spare or the door-jamb label. Do not exceed 50 mph (80 km/h) on a compact spare and use it only for short distances. Stow the flat, tools, and triangles, release the parking brake, and go straight to a tire shop. Have the flat inspected; a tire driven flat for any distance often has hidden sidewall damage and should not be reused.

warnings: Never put any part of your body under a car held up only by a jack, a pile of rocks, or a dug-out pit.
Jack only on the metal jack points shown in the owner's manual - other spots crack, bend, or let the car slip.
Do not change a tire on the traffic side of a car on a highway shoulder; get towed to a safer spot or call for help.
Tire sealant does not repair sidewall damage or blowouts, and you must tell the tire shop it is in the tire.
Compact spares are limited to about 50 mph and short distances - they are not a long-term tire.
proTips: Check the spare's pressure every month and before long trips - NHTSA advises inspecting the spare along with the other tires.
Practice one tire change in your driveway so you know where the jack points and wheel-lock key are before you need them.
A small 12-volt tire inflator and a plug kit cover many punctures that would otherwise leave you waiting for a tow.
Keep a pair of work gloves, a flashlight, and a short board for the jack base with the tire tools.

sources.title: How to Change a Tire in 11 Easy Steps
NHTSA: Never too early to prepare for driving in wintry conditions

whenNotTo: On a narrow shoulder with traffic passing close to the flat side - get the car towed or moved first.
When the jack, ground, or car feels unstable - stop and call for help rather than forcing it.
When the tire has a sidewall tear or the wheel is bent - sealant and the spare may not be enough; plan for a tow.

quickGlance.situation: You have a flat tire and need to get rolling again without getting hurt.
immediate: Hazards on, roll to a safe, level spot away from traffic
Park, parking brake, engine off, chock the opposite wheel
Set a triangle about 100 feet behind the car
then: Loosen nuts on the ground, jack at the marked point, swap, tighten in a star pattern
Keep a compact spare under 50 mph and drive to a tire shop

title: Jump Starting and Battery Troubleshooting
summary: How to tell whether a dead battery is the real problem, jump-start a car safely in the right cable order, and what to do when a jump does not work.

steps.title: Figure out what actually failed
steps.body: Turn the key or press Start and watch and listen. Rapid clicking, dim dash lights, and a slow crank point to a weak battery - a jump should help. Bright lights but one loud click and no crank can be a bad starter or a loose cable. A car that cranks normally but will not start has a fuel or spark problem, and a jump will not fix it. If the battery warning light came on while you were driving and the car then died, the charging system (alternator or belt) is the likely cause; a jump will only get you a short distance.

steps.title: Inspect the battery before touching it
steps.body: Do not jump a battery that is cracked, bulging, leaking, or smells like rotten eggs - replace it instead. Do not jump a battery that may be frozen; let it thaw first. Check that both cars use 12-volt systems (the battery label says so). Many hybrids and EVs have a small 12-volt battery that can be jumped, but AAA warns their electronics can be damaged by jumping another car - read the owner's manual, which shows the exact jump terminals. Take off rings and watches, and wear safety glasses and gloves if you have them.

steps.title: Set up both cars
steps.body: Park the good car close enough for the cables to reach without the cars touching, out of traffic and in a spot where you can be seen. Put both in Park or Neutral, set both parking brakes, and turn both ignitions and all accessories off. Clean heavy white or green corrosion off the terminals with a wire brush or a stiff rag so the clamps bite on bare metal. Route the cables away from belts and the cooling fan.

steps.title: Connect the cables in this order
steps.body: Follow the order AAA gives. (1) Red clamp to the positive (+) post of the dead battery. (2) Other red clamp to the positive (+) post of the good battery. (3) Black clamp to the negative (-) post of the good battery. (4) Last black clamp to bare, unpainted metal on the dead car's engine or frame, such as a thick bolt, away from the battery. That last connection often sparks, and a battery can give off hydrogen gas, so the spark should happen away from it. Never let the red and black clamps touch each other once any clamp is attached.

steps.title: Start the cars
steps.body: Start the good car and let it run 3 to 5 minutes; a little extra engine speed helps. Then try the dead car. If it cranks slowly but will not catch, wait about 5 minutes and try again. If it still will not start after a third try, the battery is probably finished or something else is wrong - stop before you overheat the starter. Once the dead car runs, leave the cables on for another 3 to 5 minutes.

steps.title: Disconnect in reverse and recharge
steps.body: Remove the clamps in exact reverse order: black from the engine ground, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, then red from the car you just started. Keep the clamps apart as you go. Drive the revived car for 20 to 30 minutes, with the A/C and rear defroster off if you can, so the alternator can put charge back in. Idling in a parking lot does very little. If the battery is more than about three years old or keeps dying, have it tested - a short drive will not save a worn-out battery.

steps.title: Using a portable jump starter
steps.body: A pocket lithium jump pack lets you start the car alone. Follow the pack's instructions: usually red clamp to the positive post, black clamp to the ground point or negative post, then turn the pack on and start the car within a few seconds. Most packs have reverse-polarity protection, but still double-check. Recharge the pack every few months; cold weather drains it, so keep it in the cabin during winter rather than the trunk.

warnings: Never jump a cracked, bulging, leaking, or frozen battery - it can burst and spray acid.
Connecting cables backwards can destroy fuses and computer modules; check red-to-positive before every connection.
Keep your face away from the battery while connecting and starting.
Hybrids and EVs: follow the owner's manual exactly and do not use them to jump other cars unless the manual allows it.
Never run either car in a closed garage while jumping - exhaust can kill.
proTips: A portable jump starter is one of the most useful items in a vehicle kit, since it removes the need for a second car.
If the battery light stays on after the jump, head straight to a shop or safe place - the alternator is not charging and the car will die again.
Batteries fail most in hard cold and hard heat; have yours load-tested before winter.
Write down your radio and anti-theft codes - some cars ask for them after the battery goes fully dead.

sources.title: How to Jump a Battery and Get Yourself Back on the Road
NHTSA: Never too early to prepare for driving in wintry conditions

whenNotTo: When the battery is damaged, leaking, or frozen.
When the car cranks normally but will not start - the battery is not the problem.
When the only donor is a hybrid or EV whose manual says not to jump other vehicles.

quickGlance.situation: Your car will not start and the battery seems dead.
immediate: Check the battery for cracks, leaks, bulging, or a rotten-egg smell
Both cars off, in Park, brakes set
Red to dead +, red to good +, black to good -, black to bare metal on dead car
then: Start the good car, wait 3-5 minutes, then start the dead car
Disconnect in reverse and drive 20-30 minutes; get the battery tested

title: Engine Overheating - What to Do on the Road
summary: What to do the moment the temperature gauge climbs, how to check coolant without getting burned, and how to decide between waiting for a tow and limping to safety.

steps.title: Act at the first warning
steps.body: Watch for the temperature needle climbing toward red, a coolant warning light, steam from under the hood, or a sweet smell. Turn off the air conditioning right away. If you cannot stop immediately, turning the heater and fan to full hot moves some engine heat into the cabin - open the windows and use it only as a short bridge to a safe place to stop. Slow down and avoid hard acceleration and steep climbs.

steps.title: Pull over and shut the engine off
steps.body: Turn on your hazards and get to a shoulder, side street, or parking lot. AAA advises turning the engine off as soon as you stop. Continuing to drive an engine that is overheating badly can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket, which can end the vehicle's usefulness. Get passengers out and away from traffic. If the hood is pouring steam or you see flames, stay back and call 911.

steps.title: Wait before opening anything
steps.body: The cooling system is under pressure and the coolant can be well above boiling. Never open the radiator cap or pressure cap on a hot engine - it can spray scalding coolant on your face and arms. Wait at least 30 minutes, and longer on a hot day, until the upper radiator hose is only warm and can be squeezed without resistance. Use this time to call roadside assistance, since AAA recommends a tow to a repair shop as the safe default.

steps.title: Look for the cause
steps.body: With the engine off and cool, check the see-through overflow tank for coolant level. Look under the car for green, orange, or pink puddles and trace any wet spots upward to a hose, the radiator, or the water pump. Check that the drive belt is present and tight, that the radiator fan is not broken, and that the radiator fins are not packed with leaves or bugs. Check the engine oil level too - AAA lists low oil as one cause of overheating.

steps.title: Add coolant only to a cool engine
steps.body: If coolant is low and you have no leak you can see, add the correct pre-mixed coolant to the overflow tank up to the mark, or to the radiator once it is fully cool. In a true emergency, clean water will get you to safety, but it lacks freeze and corrosion protection, so have the system flushed and refilled soon. Do not pour cold liquid into a hot engine. Open caps slowly with a thick rag, turning to the first stop and letting any pressure hiss out before removing them.

steps.title: Decide whether to drive
steps.body: AAA warns that adding coolant yourself and continuing to drive is risky, and a tow is safest. If you are somewhere unsafe and must move, drive slowly with the A/C off and the heater on, watch the gauge constantly, and stop again before it reaches red. Do not drive if you see white, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, milky oil on the dipstick, or coolant pouring out - these point to a blown head gasket or a major leak, and driving can wreck the engine in minutes.

steps.title: Prevent the next one
steps.body: Have coolant level and condition, hoses, belts, the thermostat, and the radiator cap checked before summer and winter. Replace hoses that are cracked, swollen, or soft and mushy. Carry a gallon of pre-mixed coolant or water in hot climates and on long trips. Never use coolant as a substitute for a mechanic when the gauge keeps creeping up - repeated overheating means something is failing.

warnings: Never open a hot radiator or coolant reservoir pressure cap - escaping coolant causes severe burns.
Coolant is poisonous and tastes sweet to children and pets; clean up spills and keep the jug sealed.
Stay clear of the radiator fan - many fans can start on their own even with the engine off.
Steam or smoke near the engine can be a fire; if you see flames, get everyone away and call 911.
proTips: Learn where your temperature gauge normally sits so you notice the first upward creep.
Self-fusing silicone repair tape can slow a small hose leak long enough to reach help; duct tape rarely holds on a hot, pressurized hose.
In stop-and-go traffic, shifting to neutral and lightly raising engine speed can help the fan and water pump move more coolant.
If you must use water, note it and have the coolant mix corrected before freezing weather.

sources.title: Car Overheating: 8 Causes and Solutions
Car Safety

whenNotTo: When steam or smoke is pouring out heavily - stay away and call for help.
When you see milky oil or white sweet-smelling exhaust - do not keep driving.

quickGlance.situation: The temperature gauge is climbing or steam is coming from the hood.
immediate: A/C off, heater on full hot as a short bridge
Pull over, engine off, everyone away from traffic
Do not open the radiator cap while hot
then: Wait 30+ minutes, check coolant level and leaks
Call for a tow; drive only short distances to safety while watching the gauge

title: Fuel Safety - Running Low, Refilling From Cans, and Transferring Fuel
summary: How to stretch the fuel you have, refill safely from a portable can, avoid static fires, and move fuel between containers without mouth siphoning.

steps.title: Plan so you never run dry
steps.body: Running out of fuel strands you, and on many fuel-injected cars it can also overheat or damage the in-tank fuel pump, which relies on fuel to cool it. Treat half a tank as your refill point during storm season or any time trouble may be coming - Florida's emergency managers use exactly that rule because stations run dry and lines get long before a storm. Estimate range as gallons left times realistic miles per gallon, then knock off about 20 percent for traffic, heat or cold, hills, and a loaded car.

steps.title: Stretch the fuel you have
steps.body: If the low-fuel light comes on and the next station is uncertain, slow down to a steady 45 to 55 mph (70 to 90 km/h), avoid hard acceleration and braking, turn off the A/C if it is safe to do so, and drop roof boxes or extra weight if practical. Do not shut the engine off and coast down hills - you can lose power steering and power brakes. Note the mileage when the light came on so you know how far you have gone.

steps.title: Fill portable cans on the ground
steps.body: NIOSH has documented fires caused by static electricity when gas cans are filled while sitting in a truck bed or on car carpet. Always take the can out and set it on the ground a few feet from the vehicle. Touch the can with the nozzle before you open the cap, keep the nozzle in contact with the can opening the whole time you fill, and fill no more than about 95 percent full so the fuel has room to expand. Never fill a can inside a vehicle or trunk.

steps.title: Refuel the vehicle from a can
steps.body: Shut the engine off and do not smoke or use a lighter or any flame nearby. Use the can's spout or a funnel, keep the can steady on a raised surface or your knee, and pour slowly to avoid splash-back. Many newer cars have a capless filler that needs the special funnel stored with the spare tire - keep it there. Wipe up spills and let the rag dry outdoors before storing it.

steps.title: Transfer fuel without mouth siphoning
steps.body: Never start a siphon by sucking on a hose. A mouthful of gasoline can be inhaled into the lungs and cause a serious chemical pneumonia; if anyone swallows or inhales fuel, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or 911. Use a hand-squeeze bulb siphon or a battery transfer pump, with the receiving can on the ground and lower than the source. Most modern cars have rollover and anti-siphon valves that block a hose from reaching the tank, so plan on carrying fuel in cans rather than drawing it from another car. Take fuel only from vehicles you own or have permission to use.

steps.title: Store fuel in approved containers
steps.body: Use only cans made and labeled for fuel - red for gasoline, yellow for diesel, blue for kerosene - with tight caps. Never use milk jugs, water bottles, or glass. Store cans outside the living space, in a shed or detached garage away from water heaters, furnaces, and anything that sparks, out of direct sun and out of reach of children. Do not keep a full can in the passenger area of a car. Gasoline vapors are heavier than air and can travel along the floor to a pilot light.

steps.title: Keep stored fuel fresh
steps.body: Gasoline slowly goes stale, especially ethanol blends, which can absorb water and separate. Write the fill date on every can, add a fuel stabilizer at the dose on its label if you will keep it more than a month or so, and rotate it into your car within the time the stabilizer label states. Fuel that is dark, cloudy, layered, or smells sour should not go into an engine. See the power category guide on fuel storage for longer-term storage limits.

warnings: Never start a siphon with your mouth - inhaled fuel can cause life-threatening lung injury.
Always fill portable cans on the ground, never in a truck bed, trunk, or on carpet - static sparks have caused fires.
Never carry an open or leaking can inside the passenger cabin.
Check local fire codes and your lease or HOA rules for how much fuel you may store at home.
proTips: Keep the capless-filler funnel with your gas can, not buried in the trunk well.
A cheap battery or squeeze-bulb transfer pump is much safer and faster than any hose trick.
Label each can with fuel type and date in paint pen; never mix diesel and gasoline cans.
Diesel engines that run dry may need the fuel system bled; check the owner's manual for the priming procedure.
source: NIOSH / Florida Division of Emergency Management / owner's manual guidance

sources.title: Fire Hazard from Filling Portable Gas Cans in Pickup Trucks and Cars
If You're Halfway Full, You're Halfway There
Car Safety

whenNotTo: Never siphon fuel from vehicles or tanks you do not own or have permission to use.
Do not refuel near open flame, a running engine, or a hot generator.

quickGlance.situation: You are low on fuel or need to refill from a portable can.
immediate: Slow to a steady speed and drop non-essential loads
Set gas cans on the ground before filling - nozzle touching the can
Engine off and no flames when pouring
then: Use a pump, never a mouth siphon
Store dated cans outside the living space

title: Generator Care and Troubleshooting - Keeping It Ready
summary: Simple maintenance and fixes that keep a portable generator starting when the power fails, plus the carbon monoxide rules that keep it from killing you.

steps.title: Put it outside first - CO kills fast
steps.body: CPSC reports that nearly 100 people die in the U.S. each year from generator carbon monoxide. Run a generator only outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows, and vents. Never run one in a garage, basement, shed, crawlspace, or on a porch or carport, even with doors open. Install battery-powered CO alarms on every level of the home and test them monthly. When buying, choose a model with an automatic CO shut-off feature. If a CO alarm sounds or anyone feels dizzy, sick, or confused, get everyone outside and call 911.

steps.title: Check oil before every start
steps.body: Small generator engines hold little oil and have no filter, so the level matters. With the unit level and off, check the dipstick or fill plug and top off with the oil grade the manual lists. Change new engines after the break-in time in the manual, then at the interval it gives - often every 50 to 100 hours of running, and sooner in dust or heat. Low-oil shutdown switches are a backup, not a substitute for checking.

steps.title: Keep fuel fresh and the carburetor clean
steps.body: Stale gasoline is the most common reason a stored generator will not start. It leaves gummy varnish in the small passages of the carburetor. Add a fuel stabilizer at the label dose, use ethanol-free gas if you can get it, and either run the tank dry or close the fuel valve and run the carburetor dry before long storage, as your manual directs. If it will not start after storage, drain old fuel, refill with fresh, and try again before taking it apart.

steps.title: Service the air filter and spark plug
steps.body: A clogged air filter causes hard starting, black smoke, and low power. Clean foam filters in soapy water, let them dry, and lightly re-oil if the manual says so; replace paper elements when dirty. Pull the spark plug once a season: a light tan tip is normal, black soot means running rich, and wet fuel means flooding. Replace a worn or fouled plug with the type in the manual and set the gap it specifies.

steps.title: Start a stubborn or flooded engine
steps.body: Check the basics first: fuel valve open, engine switch on, choke closed for a cold start and open for a warm one, and oil level correct. If you smell fuel and it will not catch, it is probably flooded. Turn the choke fully open, wait several minutes, and pull with the throttle open; or remove the plug, let the cylinder air out, dry the plug, and reinstall. Do not keep pulling dozens of times - you will only add more fuel.

steps.title: Refuel and connect safely
steps.body: Shut the generator off and let it cool before refueling - gasoline spilled on a hot muffler can ignite. Keep fuel cans well away from the running unit. Plug appliances in using heavy-duty outdoor extension cords rated for the load. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet to backfeed the house; that can electrocute utility workers and neighbors. Use a transfer switch or interlock installed by a licensed electrician if you want to power home circuits. Keep the unit dry, but use only covers or tents the maker approves, never an enclosure that traps exhaust.

steps.title: Test it on a schedule
steps.body: Every one to three months, start the generator and run it under a modest load for 20 to 30 minutes. This charges any starter battery, keeps seals wet, and proves it works before an outage. Log the date, run hours, and any service on a tag tied to the handle. Keep a spare spark plug, air filter, a quart of the right oil, and a funnel with the unit.

warnings: Never run a generator indoors, in a garage, or near open windows - opening doors does not prevent deadly CO buildup.
Never backfeed a house through a wall outlet; use a professionally installed transfer switch or interlock.
Refuel only when the engine is off and cool.
Keep children and pets away from a running unit and its hot muffler.
proTips: Write your generator's running and starting watt ratings on the case so anyone in the family can avoid overloading it.
A CO shut-off generator plus working CO alarms is the strongest protection you can buy.
Ethanol-free fuel (often sold for boats and small engines) stores better and reduces carburetor varnish.
Run the test under load, not idle - a no-load test hides problems.

sources.title: Winter Storm May Knock Out Power: CPSC Warns of Deadly Carbon Monoxide and Fire Risks

whenNotTo: Do not run it anywhere it cannot be at least 20 feet from occupied buildings with exhaust aimed away.
Do not operate it in standing water or with wet hands.

quickGlance.situation: You need your generator to start and run safely during an outage.
immediate: Set it outside, 20+ feet from the house, exhaust away
Check oil and use fresh fuel
CO alarms on every level of the home
then: Refuel only when off and cool
Test-run under load every 1-3 months

title: Stranded in a Vehicle in Winter - Stay Warm, Stay Found, Avoid CO
summary: What to do if snow, ice, or a crash strands you in your car in the cold: why to stay with the vehicle, how to run the engine for heat without carbon monoxide poisoning, and how to help rescuers find you.

steps.title: Stay with the vehicle
steps.body: The National Weather Service and NHTSA both say to stay in your vehicle. A car is shelter from wind and snow, and it is far easier for rescuers to spot than a person on foot. People who walk off in a blizzard can become lost or freeze within a short distance of help. Leave only if you can see a building close by, you know exactly where you are, and walking clearly improves your situation. Call 911 if you have signal, give your road, direction, mile marker or last exit, and how many people are with you, then save your phone battery.

steps.title: Clear the exhaust pipe before you run the engine
steps.body: Snow packed around the tailpipe can push carbon monoxide (CO) into the cabin. You cannot see or smell CO, and it can kill sleeping people. Before every engine run, check that the tailpipe and the area under the back of the car are clear, and clear them again after drifting snow. If you cannot reach or clear the pipe, do not run the engine. Headache, dizziness, nausea, sleepiness, or confusion in anyone are signs of CO poisoning - shut the engine off, open windows, and get fresh air.

steps.title: Run the engine for short periods only
steps.body: Run the engine and heater for about 10 minutes each hour - NWS guidance - and adjust to how much fuel you have. Open a downwind window slightly while it runs for fresh air; heavy snow and ice can seal a car tight. Use the time to warm the cabin and charge your phone. Do not fall asleep with the engine running; if there are several people, take turns staying awake. Turn the engine off between runs and close the window to hold heat.

steps.title: Hold body heat
steps.body: Put on every layer you have, especially a hat and dry socks. Wool and synthetics stay warmer when damp than cotton. Huddle together under blankets, and use floor mats, maps, or seat covers as extra insulation. Keep moving your arms, legs, fingers, and toes to make heat, but do not overexert by shoveling hard - sweat chills you later and heavy shoveling strains the heart. Eat high-calorie snacks and drink water. Do not eat snow; melting it in your mouth lowers body temperature.

steps.title: Make the car easy to find
steps.body: Tie a bright cloth - red is best - to the antenna or a door handle. At night, turn on the dome light while the engine runs so rescuers can see you, but keep it off otherwise to save the battery. Once the snow stops, raise the hood to signal that you need help. If you have flares or reflective triangles and it is safe to step out, set one behind and one in front of the car. Keep a path to one door clear so you can get out.

steps.title: Watch everyone for cold injuries
steps.body: Check each other every hour for shivering that becomes uncontrolled, slurred speech, clumsiness, confusion, or very drowsy behavior - signs of hypothermia. Look for white or grayish, hard, or numb skin on fingers, toes, ears, and nose - signs of frostbite. Warm cold hands in armpits; do not rub frostbitten skin. Infants, older adults, and anyone who is wet or injured lose heat fastest, so give them the warmest spot and extra layers. See the medical guides on hypothermia and frostbite.

steps.title: After rescue or when the storm passes
steps.body: Do not drive away until the road is open and safe; ask responders. Before driving, clear all snow off the roof, windows, and lights, and make sure the tailpipe is still clear. If anyone had CO symptoms, have them checked by a medical provider even if they feel better. Restock your winter kit right away with blankets, food, water, a shovel, a scraper, sand or cat litter, and a phone charger.

warnings: Never run the engine with a blocked tailpipe - carbon monoxide can kill everyone inside without warning.
Do not walk away from the car in a blizzard unless help is clearly in sight.
Do not sleep with the engine running.
Do not overexert shoveling; heart attacks and sweaty clothing are both real dangers in the cold.
Hybrids and plug-in hybrids may start their gas engine automatically to keep the cabin warm - keep the tailpipe clear for them too.
proTips: Keep your tank at least half full all winter - NHTSA recommends keeping it nearly full.
A battery-powered CO alarm in the glove box is cheap insurance for long winter waits.
Share your route and arrival time before leaving so someone knows where to look.
An EV can heat its cabin without exhaust; see the EV guide for stretching battery charge while stranded.

sources.title: Winter Weather Safety
NHTSA: Never too early to prepare for driving in wintry conditions
Stranded with your Vehicle

whenNotTo: When a heated building is clearly visible and reachable safely.
When the car is in immediate danger (fire, rising water, or a spot where it will be struck) - move to a safer place.

quickGlance.situation: You are stuck in your car in snow, ice, or extreme cold.
immediate: Stay with the vehicle and call 911 if you can
Clear the tailpipe before running the engine
Run the engine about 10 minutes per hour with a window cracked
then: Layer up, huddle, and keep limbs moving
Bright cloth on the antenna; raise the hood after snow stops

title: Escaping a Vehicle Sinking in Water
summary: The seconds-matter sequence for getting yourself and children out of a car that has gone into water: seatbelts, window, children, out - before calling 911.

steps.title: Know you have about one minute
steps.body: A car that lands in water usually floats for only a short time, roughly 30 to 60 seconds, before water reaches the windows. During that float time the windows can still be opened and the doors are useless because water pressure holds them shut. Do not waste it calling 911, grabbing belongings, or waiting to see what happens. AAA advises escaping first and calling for help once you are out. Remember the order: Seatbelts, Windows, Children, Out.

steps.title: Seatbelts off
steps.body: Unbuckle your own seatbelt first - you cannot help anyone while strapped in. Shout to everyone else to unbuckle. If a belt jams, cut it with a belt cutter. Keep a combined belt-cutter and window-breaker tool where you can reach it while buckled, such as clipped to the visor, on the keychain, or in the console - not in the glove box. Do not try to unbuckle children yet; you need the window open first.

steps.title: Window open - not the door
steps.body: Press the power window switch right away. Electric windows often keep working for a short time after hitting water. If the window will not open, break a side window with a spring-loaded or hammer-style escape tool, striking near a corner. AAA testing found spring-loaded tools worked better on tempered glass, and swinging a hammer is hard underwater. Do not aim at the windshield; it is laminated and will not shatter. AAA found about 1 in 3 2018 models had laminated side windows, which escape tools cannot break - check the small label in the corner of each window and know which ones are tempered.

steps.title: Children out first
steps.body: Unbuckle children starting with the oldest, and push them out the open window ahead of you. Older children can grab the roof or float briefly while you get the younger ones. For a baby or toddler in a car seat, unbuckle the harness rather than trying to lift the whole seat. Tell older kids, "Get out and hold the car," so they do not swim away into a current. Practice the order with them on dry land so the words are familiar.

steps.title: Out and up
steps.body: Go out through the window head first, pushing off the seat and door frame. Once out, climb onto the roof if the car is still floating, then swim or wade to the nearest safe shore, away from fast water. In moving water, float on your back with feet pointed downstream and steer toward shore at an angle. Once you are safe, call 911 and report the location and how many people were in the car.

steps.title: If the window cannot be opened or broken
steps.body: This is a last resort. Get everyone to an air pocket, usually toward the rear or the roof, as the car fills. When water inside nearly matches the level outside, pressure equalizes and the door may open. Take a deep breath, unlock, push the door hard, and pull yourself out along the car. This takes longer and the chance of survival drops, which is why opening or breaking a window in the first minute matters so much.

steps.title: After you get out
steps.body: Anyone who went under water, coughed hard, or feels short of breath needs medical evaluation even if they seem fine, because breathing problems can show up hours later. Get wet people warm and dry as soon as possible. Do not go back into the water for belongings. If someone is still in the car and you are not trained or equipped for water rescue, call 911 and throw something that floats rather than going in after them.

warnings: Do not call 911 before escaping - you have only seconds while the car floats.
Do not try to open the door while the car is floating; water pressure will hold it shut and waste time.
Escape tools cannot break laminated glass or the windshield - know which of your windows are tempered.
Never drive into flood water; most of these situations start with a flooded road.
proTips: Keep the escape tool within reach of the driver while buckled - visor, keychain, or console.
Rehearse "Seatbelts, Windows, Children, Out" out loud with the family.
Look for the glass label in the bottom corner of each side window when you buy a car.
In cold water, the first minute of gasping is the most dangerous - keep your head above water and focus on breathing before swimming.
source: AAA / Kids and Car Safety (based on Univ. of Manitoba research)

sources.title: Sixty Seconds: What Experts Actually Want You to Do if Your Car Sinks
Vehicle Escape Tools

whenNotTo: The "wait for the car to fill, then open the door" method is not the first choice - use it only when the windows cannot be opened or broken.

quickGlance.situation: Your car has gone into water and is starting to sink.
immediate: Seatbelts off - yours first
Window open or broken - not the door
Children out, oldest first, then you
then: Get onto the roof or to shore, then call 911
Get medical checks for anyone who swallowed or inhaled water

title: Flooded Roads - Turn Around, Don't Drown
summary: Why driving into flood water kills more people than any other flood behavior, how little water it takes to float a car, and what to do if water is rising around you.

steps.title: Know the numbers
steps.body: NWS data show flooding kills nearly 90 people a year in the U.S. on average, and more than half of those deaths happen in vehicles driven into flooded roads. It takes far less water than most people think. About 6 inches (15 cm) of water can make a car stall or lose control, and 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet. About 12 inches (30 cm) can float a small car and carry it away if the water is moving. About 18 to 24 inches (45 to 60 cm) of moving water can sweep away most vehicles, including large SUVs and pickups.

steps.title: Turn around - every time
steps.body: If water covers the road, stop well before it, turn around, and find another route. You cannot tell how deep the water is or whether the road under it is still there; floods wash out pavement and leave hidden holes. This is even harder at night. High clearance or four-wheel drive does not help - bigger vehicles float too. Do not follow another car through; theirs may have barely made it. Never drive around barricades.

steps.title: Plan routes around low ground
steps.body: When flooding is forecast, avoid low-water crossings, underpasses, dips, and roads beside creeks and rivers. Check road conditions with your state's 511 service or DOT app before you leave. If a Flash Flood Warning is issued for your area, get to higher ground now; do not wait to see water. In canyons and washes, water can arrive suddenly from rain miles away.

steps.title: If the car stalls in water
steps.body: If water is rising around a stalled car and is not flowing fast, get out right away and move to higher ground. Leave the car; it is replaceable. Do not try to restart it. If the water is moving fast, stay inside with seatbelts on until you can judge it, but be ready to escape through a window if the car starts to float. Climbing onto the roof is better than being swept away inside the car.

steps.title: If the car is swept away or starts to sink
steps.body: Act immediately: seatbelts off, window open, children out, then you. Do not try to open the door against the water. Get on the roof and call 911 once you are out. The full step-by-step is in the sinking-vehicle guide. Do not walk or swim into flowing flood water to reach shore unless staying put is clearly worse.

steps.title: After the water goes down
steps.body: Roads that have been flooded may be weakened and can collapse under a car, so drive slowly and watch for broken pavement and debris. Stay out of water near downed power lines. Do not drive a car that was submerged above the floor until it is inspected - water in the engine, fuel, or electrical system can cause failures or fire. Flood-damaged electric vehicles have an added fire risk; see the EV guide.

warnings: Never drive into water covering a road - you cannot judge depth or whether the road beneath is gone.
Never drive around a "Road Closed" barricade or flood gate.
Night makes flood water much harder to see - slow down on any road near streams in heavy rain.
Flood water may hide downed power lines and sewage - avoid wading in it.
proTips: Memorize alternate routes from home and work that stay on high ground.
If you see a flooded car with someone inside, call 911 and do not drive or wade in after them.
Turn on your weather radio or phone alerts during heavy rain events.
In flash-flood country, park facing out and away from washes so you can leave quickly.

sources.title: Flood Safety Awareness - Turn Around Don't Drown
Car Safety

whenNotTo: There is no safe depth to drive through flowing water on a road - do not try it.

quickGlance.situation: Water is covering the road ahead or rising around your car.
immediate: Stop and turn around - do not drive into the water
Pick a route on higher ground
If stalled in rising water, get out and go to high ground
then: If the car floats or sinks, follow Seatbelts, Windows, Children, Out
Have any flooded car inspected before driving it

title: Evacuation Driving - Routes, Fuel, and What to Bring
summary: How to plan and drive an evacuation: when to leave, how to pick routes, keeping fuel or charge ready, what contraflow lanes mean, and what to pack in the car.

steps.title: Leave early - when officials say go, or sooner
steps.body: Follow evacuation orders from local officials as soon as they are issued, and leave earlier if you feel unsafe. Traffic, fuel lines, and closed roads get worse by the hour. Leaving early also keeps you off roads during the worst weather, smoke, or fire. If you have elderly or disabled family members who need help evacuating, register with your local emergency office or call 2-1-1 well before storm season.

steps.title: Know where you are going
steps.body: Decide ahead of time where you will stay: friends, family, a hotel, or a public shelter. For hurricanes, Florida emergency managers point out that an evacuation often only needs to be tens of miles inland to a sturdy building out of the surge zone, not hundreds of miles. A shorter trip means less traffic and less fuel. Tell an out-of-area contact your destination and route, and check in when you arrive.

steps.title: Pick routes and backups
steps.body: Learn your area's marked evacuation routes and at least one alternate. Check your state DOT's 511 service or app for closures before and during the drive. Follow the routes officials direct you to - shortcuts and back roads may be blocked, flooded, or closed to traffic. Keep a paper road map in the car, since phone navigation may fail if cell networks are overloaded. Avoid bridges, low-lying roads, and anything near downed lines.

steps.title: Keep fuel or charge ready
steps.body: During hurricane or fire season, never let the tank drop below half - Florida calls this "If you're halfway full, you're halfway there." For EVs, Florida suggests keeping the battery between 50 and 80 percent day to day, then charging higher before you leave if a long drive is likely. Expect closed stations and long lines on the route. Carry fuel in an approved can only if it is secured outside the passenger area, such as on a hitch rack.

steps.title: Understand contraflow lanes
steps.body: For big coastal evacuations, some states reverse the inbound lanes of a highway so all lanes carry traffic away from the coast. Texas also opens extra-wide shoulders as evacuation lanes. In contraflow, exits may be few and far apart, crossovers come at set points, and you may not be able to turn back. Fill up, use the restroom, and stock food and water before you enter. Stay in your lane, follow officers and signs, and watch for stopped traffic.

steps.title: Pack the car
steps.body: Bring your go-bag for each person, water and food for at least three days, medicines and medical devices, phone chargers and a battery bank, cash, ID and copies of important documents, a first aid kit, a flashlight, and pet supplies with leashes and carriers. Load it before the order if a storm is coming. Bring a car kit with jumper cables, a tire inflator, and a spare key. Do not overload the car; heavy loads hurt braking and fuel economy.

steps.title: Drive defensively
steps.body: Expect slow, stop-and-go traffic for hours. Keep a larger gap than usual and watch for sudden stops, stalled cars, and people walking along the road. Take breaks or switch drivers when tired. Keep the radio on local news for route changes. If you break down, get as far off the road as you can, turn on hazards, and stay buckled in the car; see the highway breakdown guide.

warnings: Do not wait for the last minute - roads, fuel, and weather all get worse.
Do not drive into flood water, smoke you cannot see through, or around barricades.
Never carry gas cans inside the passenger cabin.
Do not leave pets behind in a closed home or car.
proTips: Set up a family meeting place and an out-of-area contact before you need them.
Photograph your home and belongings before leaving for insurance.
Keep an "evacuation box" by the door with chargers, documents, and medications.
Download offline maps of your area and routes before the storm.
source: Florida Division of Emergency Management / TxDOT / Ready.gov

whenNotTo: When officials say to shelter in place (for example, a hazmat release or a tornado warning) - leaving can be more dangerous.

quickGlance.situation: You may need to evacuate by car from a storm, fire, or other disaster.
immediate: Leave as soon as officials say - or earlier
Fill up or charge before the rush
Follow official routes and check 511
then: Bring go-bags, meds, documents, pets
Tell an out-of-area contact your destination

title: Building a Complete Vehicle Emergency Kit
summary: A full, layered vehicle emergency kit: the roadside basics every car needs, the survival layer for being stranded, seasonal add-ons, and how to keep it all working.

steps.title: Start with the roadside core
steps.body: These items fix or flag the most common problems: jumper cables or a charged portable jump starter; a tire inflator that plugs into the 12-volt outlet, a tire gauge, and a plug or sealant kit; reflective warning triangles or flares and a reflective vest; a flashlight or headlamp with spare batteries; work gloves; and a basic tool set with screwdrivers, pliers, an adjustable wrench, duct tape, and zip ties. Ready.gov and NHTSA both list booster cables and warning devices as car-kit basics. Check that your car's jack, lug wrench, wheel-lock key, and spare are actually there.

steps.title: Add communication and navigation
steps.body: Keep a phone charging cable that fits your car and a charged battery bank. Add a paper road map of your state and region, since cell service and navigation can fail in storms and rural areas. A small battery or hand-crank radio lets you hear emergency broadcasts if your car battery is low. Write important phone numbers - roadside assistance, insurance, family, and an out-of-area contact - on a card in the glove box. Pack a whistle for signaling.

steps.title: Pack a survival layer for being stuck
steps.body: Plan for a long wait in a closed road or traffic jam. Pack water (Cal OES suggests planning for about a gallon per person per day), high-calorie food that will not spoil such as bars and nuts, a first aid kit, a few days of any essential medicines, moist towelettes, garbage bags for waste, and a roll of toilet paper. Add a warm blanket or sleeping bag for each regular passenger, a hat and gloves, and sturdy shoes in case you must walk.

steps.title: Add winter gear
steps.body: Before the first freeze, add a snow shovel, an ice scraper and snow brush, and sand or non-clumping cat litter for traction - all items NHTSA and Ready.gov list. Add hand warmers, extra socks, a bright red cloth to tie to the antenna, and winter windshield washer fluid. Tire chains are useful where they are allowed and you have practiced putting them on. A battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm is worth adding for long waits with the engine running.

steps.title: Add hot-weather and regional items
steps.body: In hot climates, double the water, add sun shades, sunscreen, and a wide-brimmed hat, and avoid storing items that break down in heat. In wildfire or ashfall country, add NIOSH-approved N95 respirators for each person, because EPA notes dust masks and bandanas do not filter fine smoke. In flood country and anywhere near water, keep a window-breaker and seatbelt-cutter tool within the driver's reach. A small vehicle fire extinguisher, secured so it cannot roll, is useful everywhere.

steps.title: Pack and secure it right
steps.body: Use one or two sturdy bins or a duffel so you can move the kit between vehicles. Put small items in zip bags to keep them dry. Strap or wedge the kit so it cannot fly forward in a crash - loose heavy items in the cabin are dangerous. Keep the escape tool, a flashlight, and a phone charger in the cabin; everything else can go in the trunk or cargo area. Never store gasoline cans inside the passenger area.

steps.title: Keep it working
steps.body: Check the kit twice a year, such as when clocks change. Replace water and food before their dates, recharge the jump starter and battery bank, swap batteries in flashlights and radios, refill medicines, and check the spare tire's pressure. Swap in winter gear in the fall and hot-weather gear in the spring. Keep your gas tank at least half full and your car serviced - a kit is a backup, not a replacement for good maintenance.

warnings: Do not store gasoline cans or propane inside the passenger cabin.
Secure heavy items - they become projectiles in a crash.
Heat degrades batteries, medicines, and water bottles; rotate items more often in hot climates.
Check medicines for heat sensitivity and do not rely on a car kit as your only supply.
proTips: Use the app's Vehicle Kit checklist to track what you have and when it expires.
Lithium jump starters double as phone power banks.
A bright headlamp leaves both hands free for tire changes and repairs.
Pack a spare key fob or hidden key - Cal OES suggests it, and it saves you from lock-outs.
source: FEMA Ready.gov / NHTSA / NWS / Cal OES

title: Getting Unstuck From Snow, Mud, and Sand - Safely
summary: How to free a stuck vehicle with the least risk: clearing, traction aids, gentle rocking, pushing safely, and when to stop and call for help instead of risking a dangerous recovery.

steps.title: Stop spinning and check the situation
steps.body: The moment the wheels spin without moving the car, ease off the gas. Flooring it digs the tires deeper, polishes snow into ice, and can overheat the transmission. Turn on your hazards. Get out on the safe side and look at what is holding you: snow packed under the car, drive wheels in a rut, mud up to the axle, or a frame resting on a hump. Know which wheels drive your car (front, rear, or all) - the traction work goes there.

steps.title: Clear the exhaust and the wheels
steps.body: If snow is involved, clear the tailpipe first so exhaust cannot build up in the cabin while you work - AAA lists this as a key step. Then shovel or dig snow, mud, or sand away from the front and back of each drive tire and from under the car if it is high-centered. Clear a path a few feet long in the direction you want to go. Straighten the steering wheel; turned wheels plow and resist rolling.

steps.title: Add traction under the drive tires
steps.body: Put something grippy in front of the drive tires to go forward or behind them to reverse: sand, gravel, non-clumping cat litter, the car's floor mats, cardboard, branches, or a short board about 2 feet (60 cm) long. Commercial traction boards work best. Pack it tight against the tire. Warn bystanders that mats and boards can shoot out from under a spinning tire.

steps.title: Use low gear and gentle rocking
steps.body: AAA suggests turning traction control off, which lets the wheels turn enough to dig through to grip; turn it back on once you are moving. Use the lowest gear and gentle throttle. If the car moves a little and stops, rock it: ease forward as far as it goes, then shift to reverse and back up as far as it goes, building a short track. Do not shift while the wheels are still spinning, and check your owner's manual - some automatics warn against rapid rocking.

steps.title: Push only the safe way
steps.body: If others can push, have them push from the back or front at the body, never by the wheels and never standing directly behind a spinning tire, which can throw rocks, ice, and mud with great force. Keep pushers away from the tailpipe. The driver should go gently and stop at once if anyone slips. Never let anyone push near traffic on a road; get help or a tow instead.

steps.title: Mud and sand tips
steps.body: In mud, keep momentum low and steady; aggressive spinning just fills the tire tread with mud. In soft sand, some off-road drivers lower tire pressure to widen the footprint, but only do this if you have a way to re-inflate and stay within your tire maker's guidance - drive slowly on low pressure and refill before road speeds. Avoid sudden stops on soft ground, and when you stop, choose a firm or downhill spot so you can roll away.

steps.title: Know when to quit and call for help
steps.body: If the car is still stuck after a few careful tries, if it is high-centered on its frame, or if it is sliding toward a ditch, stop and call roadside assistance or a tow. Pulling a stuck vehicle with a strap or chain can be deadly: hooks, broken straps, and tow balls can fly back like bullets. If you must be towed out, use rated recovery points listed in the owner's manual, rated straps, and keep everyone far away, at least the strap's length to the side. In a storm, a stuck car is often safest as shelter - see the winter-stranding guide.

warnings: Never stand behind or beside a spinning tire - rocks, ice, and mats can be thrown hard.
Never use a tow ball or bumper as a recovery point; broken hardware can fly back and kill.
Clear the tailpipe in snow before running the engine to avoid carbon monoxide buildup.
Do not let anyone push a car near moving traffic.
proTips: Keep a folding shovel and a bag of cat litter in the trunk all winter.
Two traction boards are worth more than a long tow strap for most drivers.
Turn traction control back on once you are out - you want it on the road.
Low gear and patience beat high throttle every time.

sources.title: 7 Tips on How to Get Your Car Unstuck From Snow

Car Safety

whenNotTo: When the car is sliding toward a ditch, drop-off, or water - stop and call for help.
During a blizzard when getting out is more dangerous than staying with the car.
When the only option is an improvised strap pull from a non-rated point.

quickGlance.situation: Your car is stuck in snow, mud, or sand and the wheels just spin.
immediate: Ease off the gas and clear the tailpipe
Dig out the drive wheels and straighten the steering
Put traction material in the direction of travel
then: Low gear, gentle rocking, traction control off

title: EVs and Hybrids in Emergencies - Range, Charging, Cold, Backup Power, and Floods
summary: How to plan EV and hybrid range for evacuations and outages, what cold does to batteries, how to use your car as a safe power source, and why flooded EVs need special care.

steps.title: Plan your charge level by season
steps.body: Day to day, many owners keep the battery between about 50 and 80 percent, a range Florida's emergency managers suggest for hurricane season. When a storm, fire, or evacuation is likely, charge higher - toward 100 percent - shortly before you need it, following your owner's manual on high-charge storage. Public fast chargers slow down sharply above about 80 percent, so on a crowded route several short charges can move you faster than waiting for a full one. Expect chargers to be down or crowded during regional outages.

steps.title: Expect much less range in the cold
steps.body: AAA testing found that at 20 degrees F (-7 C) with the heater running, average EV range dropped about 41 percent; at 95 degrees F (35 C) with A/C it dropped about 17 percent. Cold slows the battery, and heating draws from the same battery. Precondition the cabin and battery while still plugged in, as DOE recommends, park in a garage or under cover, and plug in overnight in winter. Use seat and steering-wheel heaters instead of heating the whole cabin.

steps.title: If you are stranded in an EV
steps.body: An EV can keep you warm without exhaust, but only as long as the battery lasts. Turn the cabin temperature down, use seat heaters, and use "camp" or similar climate modes if your car has them. Check range every hour and leave enough to reach help when roads reopen. Hybrids and plug-in hybrids are different: many will start their gas engine automatically to heat the cabin or charge the battery, so their tailpipe must stay clear of snow just like a gas car.

steps.title: Charging when the grid is down
steps.body: Do not count on home charging during an outage unless you have a battery or solar system designed for it. Public chargers in an outage area may be offline. Use navigation or charging apps to find working stations outside the outage area. A portable generator can run a Level 1 charger slowly in a pinch, but follow both makers' instructions and every generator CO rule - outdoors, 20 feet from buildings - and expect very few miles per hour of charging.

steps.title: Use the car as a power source safely
steps.body: Many newer EVs and some hybrid trucks have built-in outlets (vehicle-to-load or V2L), commonly rated somewhere around 1.5 to 3.6 kilowatts - enough for a refrigerator, lights, fans, phones, or some medical devices. Check the owner's manual for the outlet rating and a minimum-charge setting so you do not drain the battery too low to drive. A full home-backup setup (vehicle-to-home) needs a bidirectional charger and equipment installed by a licensed electrician. Never use improvised cords or "suicide" plugs to backfeed a house - that can start fires and electrocute utility workers.

steps.title: Keep the 12-volt battery in mind
steps.body: EVs and hybrids still use a small 12-volt battery to wake up their computers. If it dies, the car may not unlock or turn on even with a full main battery. Learn where the jump points are and how to open the car manually. AAA warns hybrid and EV electronics can be damaged by jump-starting another vehicle, so do not use your EV as a donor unless the manual allows it.

steps.title: Flooded EVs: treat as a fire risk
steps.body: Saltwater is especially dangerous: it conducts electricity and corrodes battery seals, and NTSB has noted standing water around submerged packs is the key concern. After Hurricane Ian, NHTSA research found a small share of flooded EVs caught fire, sometimes after the water went down. Before flooding, move the EV to higher ground and unplug the charger. After a flood, do not drive, charge, or power anything from it until a qualified technician inspects it. NHTSA advises keeping a submerged lithium-ion vehicle at least 50 feet (15 m) from buildings and other vehicles. Call 911 for smoke, hissing or popping sounds, or flames - and stay well back.

warnings: Never backfeed a home from an EV with improvised cords; use only factory outlets or professionally installed V2H equipment.
A flooded EV, especially in saltwater, can catch fire even after the water goes down - keep it outdoors and 50+ feet from buildings.
Hybrids can start their gas engine on their own; keep the tailpipe clear and never run them in a closed garage.
Do not attempt to put out an EV battery fire yourself - get away and call 911.
proTips: Set a minimum state of charge for V2L use so you always keep enough range to evacuate.
Download offline maps and charging station lists before evacuating.
Keep a portable jump starter that works on your car's 12-volt system.
Know your car's manual door release - practice it before you need it.
source: AAA / U.S. DOE / NHTSA and NTSB flood findings / Florida DEM

title: Breaking Down on the Highway - Staying Safe on the Shoulder
summary: What to do the moment your car fails at highway speed: getting as far from traffic as possible, staying visible, deciding whether to stay in the car or get out, and calling for help.

steps.title: Get off the travel lanes
steps.body: When something fails - a warning light, a flat, a loss of power - turn on your hazard lights immediately and steer toward the right shoulder if you can (the left shoulder only if that is the only choice). If the car still rolls, aim for the next exit, a wide shoulder, or a parking area beyond a curve or hill, where drivers can see you sooner. Get as far right as possible, past the white edge line and onto the widest, firmest spot. Many states have "steer it and clear it" laws asking drivers in minor crashes to move out of travel lanes when it is safe.

steps.title: Secure the car
steps.body: Once stopped, put the car in Park, set the parking brake, and keep the hazard lights on. Turn the front wheels away from the road so a hit from behind pushes the car off the road rather than into traffic. At night, turn on the dome light too. If the engine is smoking or you smell burning, turn it off.

steps.title: Usually stay inside, buckled
steps.body: Michigan State Police and many other agencies advise staying in your car with your seat belt on while you wait for help. A seated, belted person is much better protected if another car hits the stopped vehicle. The exception: if the car is in a travel lane, on a curve with no shoulder, smoking or on fire, or at high risk of being struck, get everyone out and well away, behind a guardrail or up an embankment if one is there.

steps.title: If you must get out, do it safely
steps.body: Exit on the side away from traffic, sliding across if needed. Put on a reflective vest if you have one. Keep children and pets in hand. Stand well off the road, behind the guardrail if possible, and never stand between the car and traffic or directly behind the car. If you set warning triangles, walk facing traffic and place one about 100 feet (30 m) behind the car, with more spacing on fast roads or near curves. Do not work on the traffic side of the car - that includes changing a tire.

steps.title: Call for help
steps.body: Call roadside assistance, your insurer, or a tow company. If you are in a dangerous spot, injured, or blocking traffic, call 911. Give the highway name, direction of travel, the nearest mile marker or last exit, and a description of the car. Some states have a short code for highway help; check your state's DOT. Accept help only from uniformed officers, marked roadside service vehicles, or the tow you called. Stay in the locked car if someone you do not know stops; you can talk through a cracked window.

steps.title: Walking, if you have no choice
steps.body: Walking along a highway is dangerous and is illegal on some freeways. If you must walk, wear bright or reflective clothing, walk facing traffic as far from the road as possible, and use a flashlight at night. Never cross a highway on foot. Usually it is safer to wait with the car.

steps.title: When you are the one passing
steps.body: Every state has a Move Over law. When you see a stopped emergency, tow, or service vehicle - and in many states any stopped car with hazards - move over a full lane if you can do it safely, or slow down well below the speed limit if you cannot. Michigan, for example, requires slowing at least 10 mph below the limit. Slow down even more in rain, snow, ice, wind, or fog, when stopping distances grow.

warnings: Never stand between your car and traffic or directly behind your car on a shoulder.
Do not change a tire or make repairs on the traffic side of the car on a highway.
If the car is smoking, on fire, or in a travel lane, get everyone out and far away.
Walking on a freeway is extremely dangerous and is prohibited in some places.
proTips: Keep warning triangles and a reflective vest where you can reach them without unloading the trunk.
Note mile markers and exits as you drive so you can give your location quickly.
A roadside assistance plan through your insurer is often cheap and avoids standing on the shoulder for hours.
Keep a phone charger in the car; a dead phone turns a breakdown into an emergency.

title: Driving Through Smoke, Dust Storms, and Ashfall
summary: How to handle sudden low visibility from wildfire smoke, dust storms, and volcanic ash: when to pull aside, how to keep smoke out of the cabin, and how to protect the engine and windshield.

steps.title: Do not drive into it if you can avoid it
steps.body: The safest choice is not to enter a dust storm, heavy smoke, or ashfall at all. Check forecasts, air-quality alerts, and road reports before you leave. If you see a wall of dust ahead, or smoke dense enough to hide the road, stop well short at a safe place or take another route. If officials order an evacuation because of fire, leave early - before smoke closes roads.

steps.title: Caught in a dust storm: Pull Aside, Stay Alive
steps.body: Arizona DOT's guidance: check traffic around you and begin slowing. Pull off early, before visibility drops to nothing - leave the highway entirely if you can. Never stop in a travel lane or the emergency lane; get completely off the pavement and well away from where cars may drive. Turn off all your lights, including hazard lights, set the parking brake, and take your foot off the brake pedal. Stay inside with your seat belt on until the storm passes. Lights off matters: drivers behind you may follow your taillights and rear-end you, thinking you are still moving on the road.

steps.title: Driving in wildfire smoke
steps.body: Use low-beam headlights; high beams reflect off smoke and make it harder to see. Slow down well below the speed limit and leave three to five car lengths between you and the car ahead. Watch for emergency vehicles, wildlife, and people on foot. If the edge of the road is hard to see, use the painted right-side edge line as a guide. Put the phone away. Near an active fire, do not stop and do not drive off the road into grass or brush, where the hot exhaust system can start a fire.

steps.title: Keep smoke and dust out of the cabin
steps.body: Close all windows and vents, and set the fan to recirculate with the A/C on, as EPA advises. This cuts how much outside smoke enters. For long drives in smoke, keep a NIOSH-approved N95 respirator for each adult; it only works if it fits snugly with no gaps, and dust masks or bandanas do not filter fine smoke. N95s are not made for small children and should not be used on children under 2. People with asthma, heart disease, or lung disease should keep their medicines handy and get help if breathing worsens.

steps.title: Ashfall: drive only if you must
steps.body: USGS advises avoiding driving in volcanic ash; in heavy ashfall, drive only in an emergency. Ash is gritty, abrasive, and can be slippery like wet snow when damp. Drive slowly with headlights on and leave lots of space, since each vehicle stirs ash back into the air. Do not run the wipers on dry ash - it scratches the glass. Rinse the windshield with water and a cloth first, as often as needed.

steps.title: Protect the engine afterward
steps.body: Ash and heavy dust clog air filters and wear engine parts. USGS advises never driving without an air filter; if you cannot replace a dirty one, blow it out from the inside. In heavy ash, change oil and the oil filter far more often - USGS suggests every 50 to 100 miles (80 to 160 km) in heavy conditions and every 500 to 1,000 miles (800 to 1,600 km) in light dust. After smoke or dust, check the cabin and engine air filters, tires, and any ash buildup under the hood, and gently rinse ash off the windshield before using wipers.

warnings: Never stop in a travel lane or on the paved shoulder in a dust storm - get fully off the road with lights off.
Do not drive into grass or brush near a wildfire; a hot exhaust can ignite it.
Do not use wipers on dry ash - it can scratch the windshield badly.
Dust masks and bandanas do not protect against fine smoke particles; use a well-fitted N95.
proTips: Keep a few N95 respirators and a gallon of water for rinsing glass in the car during fire season.
Download your state's 511 or DOT app to check closures and conditions before driving.
If you live in ash or dust country, keep a spare engine air filter in the car.
A full tank lets you idle with the A/C on recirculate while waiting out dust or smoke.
source: Arizona DOT / U.S. EPA / USGS / Colorado State Patrol
